newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Australian report seen shaking up NZ banks.
newsitem.headline: Australian report seen shaking up NZ banks.

text.p: Australia's upcoming Wallis report into its financial system is set to prompt a shakeout in New Zealand's crowded banking industry, analysts said on Friday.
Four of the six main retail banks here are Australian-owned.

"Whatever happens in Australia, it will have an impact in New Zealand. It's going to be interesting times," Andrew Dinsdale, chairman of the finance and banking group of New Zealand accountancy firm KPMG, told Reuters.
Australian Treasurer Peter Costello has said he expects to release the recommendations from the Wallis inquiry next week.
The inquiry, established by the government and headed by prominent businessman Stan Wallis, is the first major review of Australian finance sector regulations since the early 1980s.

Its report is expected to include a recommendation to end a policy, known as the "six pillars" and set by the former Labor government, which prevents mergers between the four big Australian banks and the two largest life offices.
It is also expected to recommend scrapping takeover provisions that make it difficult for foreign banks to move into Australian retail banking in a big way.

Speculation is rife in New Zealand's crowded marketplace about who might take over whom in Australasia, with National Australia Bank, the largest and most profitable of the major Australians, seen as the most likely buyer.
NAB owns the large Bank of New Zealand group.

Westpac Banking Corp, owner of WestpacTrust in New Zealand, and the Australia and New Zealand Banking Group, are the most frequently touted as seeming vulnerable to takeover bids if merger rules are eased.

KPMG's Dinsdale said the picture might have changed after Westpac's announcement on Thursday of an A$1.435 billion takeover bid for the Bank of Melbourne, which should strengthen its balance sheet and make it a less likely target.
In New Zealand the Commerce Commission (NZCC) monopolies watchdog is seen likely to give sector takeovers the green light on the basis that the national market is so highly-competitive.
Analysts such as Massey University professor of banking Chris Moore point to a Bank of New Zealand/ANZ link-up as the only exception the commission might find hard to stomach.
That would throw together two of the largest domestic market players.
Dinsdale said NAB or ANZ might have to divest some New Zealand interests under that scenario, but Moore said other competition should still be strong enough to pacify the NZCC.
"A merger (of ANZ) with NAB would still make a very big bank here, but not impossible, in terms of the merger rules at the moment in the Commerce Commission," he said.
New Zealand, with a population of 3.5 million, has 411 bank branches per million people, compared with 402 in Australia, 250 in Britain, and 228 in the United States.

While NAB tops the list of probable buyers of Australasian banks, analysts are not discounting the possibility of aggressive groups such as Hongkong Shanghai Banking Corp or Deutsche Bank AG picking off a major regional player without too much trouble.
The future of Lloyds TSB-owned National Bank of New Zealand is another coming under scrutiny.

Moore said National had been caught out a year ago when it was pipped at the post by Westpac in its bid for Trust Bank. Analysts suggested at the time the failure to acquire Trust Bank might prompt Lloyds to review its position in New Zealand.

Dinsdale suggested ASB Bank, owned by the Commonwealth Bank of Australia would be a natural buyer if National came up for sale. The Bank of Scotland, through its Countrywide Bank, might also be interested.
